content: 1. The use of prophylactic antibiotics for women in preterm labor with ruptured membranes was associated with a reduction of 30 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 7 fewer to 50 fewer cases). The evidence quality was rated as high and deemed critical. However, the confidence interval was wide, crossing the line of no effect, and there was significant statistical heterogeneity (I² > 60%). 2. Neonatal encephalopathy was evaluated in one randomized trial, with no events reported in either the intervention or control groups (0/30 in both). The evidence quality was rated as very low and critical due to serious design limitations, small sample size, and lack of events. 3. Prophylactic antibiotics for women with prelabor rupture of membranes at or near term showed a reduction of 23 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 46 fewer to 5 more cases). The evidence quality was high and critical. However, the confidence interval crossed the line of no effect, and the pooled effect was derived from studies with design limitations. 4. For neonatal mortality with early induction of labor, one randomized trial reported no events in either group (0/820 in both). The evidence quality was low and critical due to very serious design limitations and a lack of events. 5. For neonatal mortality with late induction of labor, one randomized trial reported no events in either group (0/55 in the intervention group and 0/50 in the control group). The evidence quality was very low and critical due to serious design limitations and a lack of events. 6. Prophylactic antibiotics for women with meconium-stained amniotic fluid during labor showed no significant effect, with a reduction of 0 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 40 fewer to 188 more cases). The evidence quality was low and critical due to design limitations, wide confidence intervals, small sample size, and few events. 7. Prophylactic antibiotics for women undergoing manual removal of retained placenta showed a reduction of 11 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 45 fewer to 56 more cases). The evidence quality was very low and critical due to serious design limitations and wide confidence intervals. 8. Prophylactic antibiotics for women undergoing operative vaginal deliveries (randomized controlled trials) showed an increase of 41 cases per 1,000. The evidence quality was low and important due to design limitations and wide confidence intervals. 9. Routine prophylactic antibiotics for women undergoing operative vaginal deliveries (non-randomized studies) showed a reduction of 4 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 6 fewer to 40 more cases). The evidence quality was very low and critical due to design limitations and wide confidence intervals. 10. Routine prophylactic antibiotics for women with thirdand fourth-degree perineal tears showed a reduction of 119 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 167 fewer to 17 more cases). The evidence quality was very low and critical due to high loss to follow-up, small sample size, and wide confidence intervals. 11. Routine prophylactic antibiotics for women with uncomplicated vaginal birth showed an increase of 1 case per 1,000. The evidence quality was very low and critical due to serious design limitations, significant statistical heterogeneity (I² > 60%), and wide confidence intervals. 12. Vaginal cleansing with an antiseptic agent prior to cesarean section (all women) showed a reduction of 5 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 15 fewer to 12 more cases). The evidence quality was moderate and important due to design limitations and wide confidence intervals. 13. Vaginal cleansing with an antiseptic agent prior to cesarean section (by presence of labor) showed a reduction of 4 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 43 fewer to 53 more cases). The evidence quality was moderate and critical due to wide confidence intervals. 14. Vaginal cleansing with an antiseptic agent prior to cesarean section (by status of membranes) showed a reduction of 9 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 46 fewer to 44 more cases). The evidence quality was moderate and critical due to wide confidence intervals. 15. Preoperative skin preparation with alcohol scrub plus iodophor drape versus iodophor scrub alone showed an increase of 48 cases per 1,000. The evidence quality was low and important due to small sample size and wide confidence intervals. 16. Preoperative skin preparation with chlorhexidine gluconate versus povidone-iodine showed a reduction of 373 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 145 fewer to 451 fewer cases). The evidence quality was very low and important due to design limitations, small sample size, and wide confidence intervals. 17. Preoperative skin preparation with parachlorometaxylenol plus iodine versus iodine alone showed a reduction of 77 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 282 fewer to 243 more cases). The evidence quality was low and critical due to wide confidence intervals and small sample size. 18. The method of application of antiseptic agents for preoperative skin preparation (drape versus no drape) showed an increase of 46 cases per 1,000. The evidence quality was moderate and important due to design limitations and wide confidence intervals. 19. The method of application of antiseptic agents for preoperative skin preparation (alcohol with drape versus iodophor without drape) showed an increase of 48 cases per 1,000. The evidence quality was low and important due to small sample size and wide confidence intervals. 20. Prophylactic antibiotics for women undergoing cesarean section (any antibiotic) showed a reduction of 28 cases per 1,000. The evidence quality was moderate and important due to design limitations. 21. Prophylactic antibiotics for women undergoing cesarean section (by class of antibiotics) showed a reduction of cases, but the evidence quality and specific effect estimates were not provided in the excerpt.
